claim: Whole exome sequences have now been collected for millions of humans.
source: Whole exome sequences have now been collected for millions of humans, with the related goals of identifying pathogenic mutations in patients and establishing reference repositories of data from unaffected individuals.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a factual statement about the current state of data collection.

claim: CpG sites that are methylated in the germline experience mutations to T at an elevated rate of ~10-7 per site per generation.
source: Here, we focus on CpG sites that are methylated in the germline and experience mutations to T at an elevated rate of ~10-7 per site per generation
evidence: This mutation rate is stated in the abstract and supported by de novo mutation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Approximately 99% of methylated CpG sites harbor a C/T polymorphism when considering synonymous mutations in a sample of 390,000 individuals.
source: considering synonymous mutations in a sample of 390,000 individuals, ~ 99 % of such CpG sites harbor a C/T polymorphism.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by polymorphism data analysis.

claim: At current sample sizes, not seeing a non-synonymous polymorphism at a methylated CpG site is indicative of strong selection against that mutation.
source: Methylated CpG sites provide a natural mutation saturation experiment for fitness effects: as we show, at current sample sizes, not seeing a non-synonymous polymorphism is indicative of strong selection against that mutation.
evidence: This is a key inference drawn from the saturation observation and statistical analysis.

claim: Approximately 27% of possible loss-of-function mutations at methylated CpG sites are likely to be highly deleterious.
source: We rely on this idea in order to directly identify a subset of CpG transitions that are likely to be highly deleterious, including ~27 % of possible loss-of-function mutations
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the analysis of segregating vs. invariant sites.

claim: Up to 20% of possible missense mutations at methylated CpG sites are likely to be highly deleterious, depending on the type of functional site in which they occur.
source: and up to 20 % of possible missense mutations, depending on the type of functional site in which they occur.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by functional site analysis in Figure 2.

claim: Most mutation types, with rates on the order of 10-8 or 10-9, remain very far from saturation at current sample sizes.
source: Unlike methylated CpGs, most mutation types, with rates on the order of 10-8 or 10-9, remain very far from saturation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated through simulation and data analysis in Figure 3.

claim: The spontaneous deamination of methyl-cytosine underlies the uniquely high rate of C > T mutations at methylated CpG sites.
source: An attractive feature of methylated CpG (mCpG) sites is that a single mechanism, the spontaneous deamination of methyl-cytosine, is believed to underlie the uniquely high rate of C > T mutations at these sites (Duncan and Miller, 1980)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Duncan and Miller, 1980.

claim: Germline methylation at CpG sites is strongly predictive of their mutability.
source: thus, germline methylation at CpG sites is strongly predictive of their mutability (Kong et al., 2012; Jónsson et al., 2017; Gao et al., 2019; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The mean haploid, autosomal C > T mutation rate at methylated CpG sites is 1.17 × 10–7 per generation.
source: For these ~1.1 million sites (of 1.8 million total CpG sites in sequenced exons), we calculate a mean haploid, autosomal C > T mutation rate of 1.17 × 10–7 per generation using de novo mutations (DNMs) in a sample of ~2900 sequenced parent-offspring trios (Materials and methods, Figure 1—figure supplements 1–2, Halldorsson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is calculated from de novo mutation data from Halldorsson et al., 2019.

claim: CpG transitions differ somewhat in their mutation rates based on their trinucleotide context.
source: Notably, CpG transitions differ somewhat in their mutation rates based on their trinucleotide context (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a; Aggarwala and Voight, 2016)
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 3a and citation to Aggarwala and Voight, 2016.

claim: CpG transitions are consistently an order of magnitude higher in mutation rate than the genome average.
source: even so, they are consistently an order of magnitude higher than the genome average (Kong et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kong et al., 2012.

claim: There is no appreciable difference in average DNM rates between methylated CpGs inside and outside exons.
source: Nonetheless, considering methylated CpGs inside and outside exons, which differ in a number of these features, there is no appreciable difference in average DNM rates (Fisher Exact Test (FET) p-value = 0.1, Figure 1—figure supplement 4a).
evidence: This is supported by statistical test (FET p-value = 0.1) and Figure 1—figure supplement 4a.

claim: The rate at which two DNMs occur at the same methylated CpG site is not significantly different for sites inside versus outside exons.
source: Similarly, the rate at which two DNMs occur at the same site, a summary statistic that reflects the variance in mutation rates, is not significantly different for methylated CpGs inside versus outside exons (FET p-value = 0.35; Figure 1—figure supplement 4b).
evidence: This is supported by statistical test (FET p-value = 0.35) and Figure 1—figure supplement 4b.

claim: 94.7% of all possible synonymous CpG transitions at methylated sites are observed in the gnomAD data alone.
source: At these sites, 94.7 % of all possible synonymous CpG transitions are observed in the gnomAD data alone
evidence: This is directly calculated from gnomAD polymorphism data.

claim: 98.8% of all possible synonymous CpG transitions at methylated sites are observed in the combined sample including gnomAD, UK Biobank, and DiscovEHR datasets.
source: and 98.8 % in the combined sample including all three datasets (Figure 1).
evidence: This is directly calculated from combined polymorphism data and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Even in the least mutable CpG trinucleotide context, 98% of putatively neutral sites are segregating in current samples.
source: Even in the least mutable CpG trinucleotide context, 98 % of putatively neutral sites are segregating in current samples (Figure 1—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3b.

claim: In the absence of selection, almost every methylated CpG site would be segregating a T at current sample sizes.
source: These observations imply that in the absence of selection, almost every methylated CpG site would be segregating a T at current sample sizes
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the high saturation levels observed.

claim: Not seeing a T allele at a methylated CpG site provides strong evidence it was removed by selection.
source: and further that not seeing a T provides strong evidence it was removed by selection.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the saturation observation.

claim: At current sample sizes, there is a substantial amount of information about whether individual CpG transitions are deleterious.
source: Thus, at current sample sizes, there is a substantial amount of information about whether individual CpG transitions are deleterious.
evidence: This is an inference based on the saturation analysis and FDR calculations.

claim: In a smaller sample with only 10% of putatively neutral sites segregating, there is almost no information about selection in observing individual sites to be invariant.
source: By contrast, in a smaller sample with only 10 % of putatively neutral sites segregating, there is almost no information about selection in observing individual sites to be invariant (p ≤ 0.9).
evidence: This is a theoretical calculation demonstrating the importance of sample size.

claim: The mean de novo mutation rates do not differ for synonymous sites and for various non-synonymous annotations at methylated CpG sites.
source: While we cannot examine whether the distributions of mutation rates are identical for lack of data, we verify that the mean de novo mutation rates do not differ for synonymous sites and for various non-synonymous annotations (Figure 2a)
evidence: This is verified through analysis shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The distributions of methylation levels are similar for synonymous and non-synonymous sites, with a significant but small shift towards higher methylation for non-synonymous sites.
source: we also check that the distributions of methylation levels (conditional on ≥65%), an important determinant of mutation rates, are similar for synonymous and non-synonymous sites (with a significant but small shift towards higher methylation and thus presumably higher mutation rates for non-synonymous sites; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: All categories of missense, loss-of-function, and regulatory variants show a significant depletion in the fraction of segregating sites compared to synonymous variants.
source: All categories of missense, loss-of-function, and regulatory variants show a significant depletion in the fraction of segregating sites compared to synonymous variants (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2b with statistical significance.

claim: There is approximately a 27% deficit of loss-of-function variants at methylated CpG sites compared to what would be expected under neutrality.
source: These data therefore suggest that there are ~27 % fewer loss-of-function variants than would be expected under neutrality
evidence: This is calculated from the data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: At invariant sites within the LOF annotation, neutrality can be rejected at an FDR of only 4.4%.
source: at invariant sites within this annotation, neutrality can be rejected at an FDR of only 4.4 % ( = 1.2/27).
evidence: This is calculated from the deficit of LOF variants.

claim: A 27% deficit of loss-of-function variants is seen even when sites are matched for predicted level of linked selection.
source: A 27 % deficit of loss-of-function variants is again seen if we match the sites to synonymous mutational opportunities with the same predicted level of linked selection, i.e., with similar genealogical histories (McVicker et al., 2009; Figure 2—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2a after matching for B-statistics.

claim: When comparing CpG sites at which mutations lead to protein-truncation in the first versus the second half of transcripts, approximately the same number are missing mutations relative to synonymous sites in both subsets.
source: Supporting the widely used assumption that LOF mutations within a gene are equivalent (after filtering for those at the end of transcripts; Karczewski et al., 2020; Cassa et al., 2017), when we compare the set of CpG sites at which mutations are annotated as leading to protein-truncation in the first versus the second half of transcripts, approximately the same number are missing mutations relative to synonymous sites in both subsets (Figure 2—figure supplement 3; FET p-value = 0.9).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 with FET p-value = 0.9.

claim: The fraction of missense mutations and splice region variants not observed in current samples is about 5.3%, with an FDR of 22.6%.
source: By comparison, the fraction of missense mutations and splice region variants not observed in current samples is only about 5.3%, and the FDR 22.6 % ( = 1.2/5.3) (whether or not we match for the effects of linked selection; see Figure 2—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is calculated from the data and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2a.

claim: For missense mutations at sites that may disrupt or alter DNA-binding, there is a ~12–20% deficit in segregating sites relative to synonymous sites.
source: For the subset of sites at which missense mutations may disrupt or alter binding, particularly DNA-binding, there is a ~ 12–20% deficit in segregating sites relative to what is seen at synonymous sites
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2c-d.

claim: The fraction of sites segregating is inversely proportional to the predicted functional importance of the sites using CADD scores.
source: We can also check that the fraction of sites segregating is inversely proportional to the predicted functional importance of the sites using CADD scores (Rentzsch et al., 2019), widely used measures of constraint that incorporate functional annotations and measures of conservation. Across deciles, mean de novo transition rates at methylated CpGs are similar (Figure 2—figure supplement 5a) and, as expected, the fraction of segregating sites decreases with increasing CADD scores (Figure 2—figure supplement 5b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5a and 5b.

claim: For sites with mutation rate on the order of 10-9, the fraction of possible synonymous sites that segregate in a sample of 780K chromosomes is very low (5% for T > A mutations).
source: For sites with mutation rate on the order of 10–9, which is the case for the vast majority of non-CpGs, the fraction of possible synonymous sites that segregate in a sample of 780K chromosomes is very low: for instance, it is 5 % for T > A mutations, which occur at an average rate of 1.2 × 10–9 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3a and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: For C > T mutations not at methylated CpGs (rate 0.9 × 10–8), 27% of synonymous sites segregate in a sample of 780K chromosomes.
source: and 27 % even for other C > T mutations, which occur at a rate of 0.9 × 10–8 per site (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), compared to ~99 % for C > T mutations at methylated CpGs (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3a and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: For invariant sites of less mutable types, there is little information with which to evaluate the fit to the neutral null in current samples.
source: For invariant sites of these less mutable types, there is little information with which to evaluate the fit to the neutral null in current samples.
evidence: This is an inference based on the low saturation levels for these mutation types.

claim: The average length of the genealogy for 390K individuals is substantially shorter than 100 million generations.
source: The observation that mutation types with rates on the order of 10–8 are far from saturation further indicates that the average length of the genealogy for these 390K individuals is substantially shorter than 100 million generations.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of saturation for these mutation types.

claim: Under a demographic model with Ne = 10 million for the past 50 generations, a sample of 780K chromosomes has a genealogy spanning an average of 34 million generations.
source: Consistent with the rough estimate above, under our choice of demographic model, a sample of 780K chromosomes has a genealogy spanning an average of 34 million generations (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: This is calculated from simulations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: Increasing the number of samples by a factor of 12 only increases the average tree length approximately 3.3 times.
source: Indeed, increasing the number of samples by a factor of 12 only increases the average tree length ~3.3 x (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a,b)
evidence: This is shown through simulations in Figure 3b and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: A site that mutates at rate 10-9 per generation is expected to have experienced ~0.04 mutations in the genealogical history of a sample of ~1 million.
source: thus, a site that mutates at rate 10–9 per generation is expected to have experienced ~0.04 mutations in the genealogical history of a sample of ~1 million, and 0.1 mutations in a sample of 10 million.
evidence: This is calculated from the genealogy length and mutation rate.

claim: Saturation for mutation rates of 10-8 or 10-9 per site per generation may not be achievable any time soon.
source: The implication is that saturation for mutation rates of 10–8 or 10–9 per site per generation may not be achievable any time soon.
evidence: This is an inference based on the slow growth of genealogy length with sample size.

claim: Samples that combine individuals from more diverse genetic ancestries have longer genealogical histories.
source: Moreover, for simplicity, we model one or at most two populations, when samples that combine individuals from more diverse genetic ancestries have longer genealogical histories (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c; see Figure 1) and thus capture more variation.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c.

claim: In current samples of 780K chromosomes, the posterior odds for invariant methylated CpGs having hs ≥ 0.5 × 10–3 are 92%.
source: In current samples, the posterior odds for invariant methylated CpGs having hs ≥ 0.5 × 10–3 are 92 % under our model, whereas they are 37 % for segregating methylated CpGs.
evidence: This is calculated from Bayesian inference using simulations.

claim: The fraction of de novo LOF mutations at methylated CpGs with hs ≥ 0.5 × 10–3 is roughly 52%.
source: Considering possible LOF mutations at methylated CpGs, of which 27 % are not observed in current samples, these odds imply that the fraction of de novo LOF mutations with hs ≥ 0.5 × 10–3 is roughly 52 % ( = 0.27 × 0.92 + 0.73 × 0.37).
evidence: This is calculated by weighting posterior odds by the fraction of segregating and invariant sites.

claim: The fraction of de novo missense mutations at methylated CpGs estimated to be highly deleterious is 40%.
source: For missense sites, given the same uninformative prior on hs as for LOF mutational opportunities, the fraction estimated to be highly deleterious is 40 % ( = 0.05 × 0.92 + 0.95 × 0.37).
evidence: This is calculated by weighting posterior odds by the fraction of segregating and invariant sites.

claim: Approximately 0.97% of all de novo point mutations are missense and ~0.07% lead to a LOF.
source: Since ~0.97 % of all de novo point mutations are missense and ~0.07 % lead to a LOF (see Methods)
evidence: This is calculated from de novo mutation data.

claim: There is roughly a 1 in 236 chance that a de novo mutation has an effect hs ≥0.5 × 10–3.
source: these estimates translate into roughly a 1 in 236 chance ( = 40%x0.97% + 52% x0.07%) that a de novo mutation has an effect hs ≥0.5 × 10–3.
evidence: This is calculated from the fractions of deleterious missense and LOF mutations.

claim: Assuming each individual inherits 70 new mutations, one out of every 3.4 individuals is born with a new and potentially highly deleterious, non-synonymous mutation.
source: Assuming, finally, that each individual inherits 70 new mutations (Kong et al., 2012; Jónsson et al., 2017), these estimates imply that one out of every 3.4 individuals is born with a new and potentially highly deleterious, non-synonymous mutation.
evidence: This is calculated from the probability of a deleterious mutation and the number of mutations per individual.

claim: In a sufficiently large sample, even a segregating site can be subject to strong selection.
source: In a sufficiently large sample, even a segregating site can be subject to strong selection (Figure 4a and b).
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations shown in Figure 4a and b.

claim: In current exome sample sizes, a C > T mutation at a methylated CpG site with hs = 0.5 × 10–3 is almost always observed segregating.
source: For instance, in current exome sample sizes, a C > T mutation at a methylated CpG site with hs = 0.5 × 10–3 is almost always observed segregating (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is shown through simulations in Figure 4c.

claim: Under mutation-selection-drift balance in a constant population size, a mutation that arises at rate 1.2 × 10–7 per generation and is removed by selection at rate hs = 0.05% per generation has an expected population frequency of 2.4 × 10–4.
source: This follows from the expectation under mutation-selection-drift balance (Gillespie, 1998): in a constant population size, a mutation that arises at rate 1.2 × 10–7 per generation and is removed by selection at rate hs = 0.05% per generation has an expected population frequency of 2.4 × 10–4
evidence: This is calculated from mutation-selection-drift balance theory.

claim: In a sample of 780K, a mutation with hs = 0.05% has a mean number of 187 copies.
source: in a sample of 780K, the mean number of copies is 187.
evidence: This is calculated from the expected population frequency.

claim: Segregating sites in large samples are a mixture of neutral, weakly selected and strongly selected sites.
source: Thus, segregating sites in large samples are a mixture of neutral, weakly selected and strongly selected sites.
evidence: This is an inference from the mutation-selection-drift balance analysis.

claim: As samples grow in size, it cannot simply be assumed that clinically relevant variants are absent from reference datasets.
source: An implication is that, although large reference repositories such as gnomAD were partly motivated by the possibility of excluding deleterious variants, as samples grow in size, it cannot simply be assumed that clinically relevant variants are absent from reference datasets.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that strongly selected mutations can segregate in large samples.

claim: The only mutations never seen as samples grow in size would be the ones that are embryonically lethal.
source: In principle, the only mutations never seen as samples grow in size would be the ones that are embryonically lethal.
evidence: This is a theoretical inference about the limit of large sample sizes.

claim: At current sample sizes, invariant methylated CpGs are likely highly deleterious.
source: At current sample sizes, invariant methylated CpGs are likely highly deleterious
evidence: This is an inference from the saturation analysis and Bayesian inference.

claim: For less mutable types, the information content at invariant sites is very limited at even the largest sample sizes considered.
source: for less mutable types, the information content at invariant sites is very limited at even the largest sample sizes considered (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Mutations classified as pathogenic in ClinVar or identified as underlying severe developmental disabilities in the DDD cohort are 6-fold to 51-fold enriched at sites invariant in 390K individuals compared to those classified as benign.
source: Accordingly, mutations classified as pathogenic in ClinVar (Landrum et al., 2018) or identified as underlying severe developmental disabilities in the Deciphering Developmental Disorders (DDD) cohort (Kaplanis et al., 2020) are 6-fold to 51-fold enriched at sites invariant in 390K individuals compared to those classified as benign (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 using ClinVar and DDD data.

claim: The de novo mutation data used in this study comes from ~190,000 published de novo mutations in a sample of 2976 parent-offspring trios that were whole genome sequenced.
source: We focused on ~190,000 published de novo mutations in a sample of 2976 parent-offspring trios that were whole genome sequenced (Halldorsson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The trio dataset used is the largest publicly available set of trios that have not been sampled on the basis of a disease phenotype.
source: To date, this is the largest publicly available set of trios that, to our knowledge, have not been sampled on the basis of a disease phenotype.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Methylated CpG sites are defined as those that are methylated ≥65% of the time in both testes and ovaries.
source: Here, we define 'methylated' CpG sites in exons as those that are methylated ≥65 % of the time in both testes and ovaries.
evidence: This is the operational definition used in the study.

claim: There are approximately 1.1 million methylated CpG sites out of 1.8 million total CpG sites in sequenced exons.
source: For these ~1.1 million sites (of 1.8 million total CpG sites in sequenced exons)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: All but 12% of segregating mCpG transitions were shared across at least two non-overlapping datasets.
source: All but 12 % of segregating mCpG transitions were shared across at least two non-overlapping datasets.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section as a quality check.

claim: Of segregating variants seen in one of the gnomAD or UK Biobank datasets, all but two variants had at least 5% of individuals sequenced at that position.
source: Of segregating variants seen in one of the gnomAD or UK Biobank datasets, all but two variants had at least 5 % of individuals (and typically on the order of ~100 K) sequenced at that position.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section as a quality check.
